blanks.subject: People's Bank of China — completeness of its counterparty list
blanks.text: The PBoC's own table 'Status of Bilateral Local Currency Swap Agreements Signed by PBoC (As of September 30, 2025)' was fetched with curl and read as raw text. It lists 32 counterparties and nothing else: Hong Kong 8,000; Korea 4,000; Indonesia 4,000; European Central Bank 3,500; United Kingdom 3,500; Singapore 3,000; Canada 2,000; Australia 2,000; Japan 2,000; Brazil 1,900; Malaysia 1,800; Switzerland 1,500; Russia 1,500; Argentina 1,300; Thailand 700; Chile 500; Saudi Arabia 500; Hungary 400; Qatar 350; Turkey 350; United Arab Emirates 350; Macao 300; South Africa 300; Pakistan 300; New Zealand 250; Egypt 180; Mongolia 150; Nigeria 150; Sri Lanka 100; Laos 60; Iceland 35; Mauritius 20 (unit: RMB 100 million). Every one of those 32 is already filed in swaps.json, so there is nothing new to add from the PBoC and the row's largest provider is exhausted at the counterparty level.

blanks.subject: People's Bank of China — twelve counterparties that are filed but are NOT on the PBoC's current table
blanks.text: Comparing the PBoC's own 30 September 2025 table against swaps.json, twelve counterparties already filed do not appear on it: Albania, Armenia, Belarus, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Morocco, Nepal, Serbia, Suriname, Tajikistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. That is good evidence those lines have lapsed rather than that they never existed, and the filed records for them carry status 'unknown'. I did not re-file them as lapsed, because that would duplicate existing rows; a future round could update status in place. One caution: the Serbia record filed with date 2026-05-28 post-dates the table, so Serbia's absence from a September-2025 table says nothing about it.

blanks.subject: Federal Reserve — current and temporary arrangements
blanks.text: The New York Fed's 'Central Bank Swap Arrangements' page was fetched with curl and read in full as raw text. It names exactly five standing counterparties (Bank of Canada, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, European Central Bank, Swiss National Bank) in place since 31 October 2013, plus the 1994 NAFA lines of USD 2 billion with the Bank of Canada and USD 3 billion with the Bank of Mexico and Mexico's USD 9 billion NAFA line with the US Treasury. The linked archive page ('Central Bank Liquidity Swaps Arrangements Archive') carries only the 2010-2013 documentation for those same five. No further counterparty is named anywhere on either page, so the Fed's 17 filed records plus the 1962-1998 network added this round exhaust what the Fed publishes.

blanks.subject: Arab Monetary Fund — does not belong in this row
blanks.text: The AMF's own 2025 annual report (179,011 characters) was read through the fetch tool. It carries no membership roster, says only that 'The Fund's membership currently includes all Arab countries that are members of the League of Arab States', and describes its lending as loans to governments and ministries of finance — 'signed with the Government of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan' is the pattern — not as swap or repo lines with member central banks. Filing 22 Arab states into this row on AMF membership would have been a fabrication of instrument type, so nothing was filed. If a future round wants the AMF, the thing to look for is the AMF's Articles of Agreement and whether subscriptions are paid by central banks, which is a different claim.

blanks.subject: IRL and VEN — swap lines the FOMC refused
blanks.text: The Cleveland Fed / NBER history of the Fed swap lines states that 'The FOMC rejected requests for swap lines from Ireland, primarily because that country was too small in terms of its international trade and financial dealings and from Venezuela primarily because that country was not compliant with Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement on currency convertibility'. So Ireland asked and was refused, which is a documented blank rather than an untested country. Venezuela was refused by the Fed but is in the denominator by another route, as a founding member of the Andean Reserve Fund / FLAR.

blanks.subject: ECB repo lines — Serbia, and the full 2020 repo set
blanks.text: The ECB's old repo-lines page (/mopo/liquidity-lines/repo-lines/html/index.en.html) now returns 'Sorry, this page does not exist': the ECB consolidated all repo facilities into EUREP in its 16 January 2024 framework review, and the chronology page carries narrative only, with no country list. swaps.json already holds the seven counterparties from the ECB's 15 December 2022 extension (Albania, Andorra, Hungary, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, San Marino). A 2020 repo line with the National Bank of Serbia is very likely and was not opened in this round; Serbia is in the denominator anyway through the PBoC.

blanks.subject: Nordic swap lines to Iceland, 2008
blanks.text: The Central Bank of Iceland's own pages at cb.is for '2008-05-16 The Central Bank of Iceland concludes swap facility arrangements' and '2008-11-20 Nordic central banks extend currency swap agreements' were fetched with curl and returned a 6.4 KB JavaScript shell with no article text, so the Danish, Norwegian and Swedish lines to Iceland were not actually read and no amount is claimed. Iceland is in the denominator through the PBoC, and Denmark, Norway and Sweden through the Fed, so this gap costs the denominator nothing.

blanks.subject: The euro area is the denominator's biggest soft spot
blanks.text: This row keys the ECB's arrangements to 'EMU', and a union key expands to every member, so one ECB record puts a swap line in all twenty euro-area boxes. That is probably where most of the gap between the 64 distinct jurisdictions actually filed in swaps.json and the map's '44% of 192' (about 85 places) comes from. Of the twenty, only six are shown here to have ever held a line of their own: Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, through the Fed's 1962-1998 network, plus Estonia and Latvia through the Riksbank and Croatia through the ECB's 2020 precautionary line. For Spain, Portugal, Ireland, Greece, Finland, Luxembourg, Slovenia, Slovakia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta no line of their own was found, and in Ireland's case the FOMC is recorded refusing one. Whether a euro-area member 'has a swap line' through the Eurosystem is a judgement for the map's owner, not something a source settles; it should be decided explicitly rather than by the union-key expansion.

checked_not_in_assignment.subject: ECB-PBoC and ECB-Federal Reserve as ECB-side records
checked_not_in_assignment.text: The ECB's current list gives its renminbi swap line a maximum borrowable amount of EUR 45,000 million (CNY 350 billion when renminbi are provided to the ECB) and an expiry date of 8 October 2028, and its Federal Reserve, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan, Swiss National Bank and Bank of England lines as unlimited and standing. Both arrangements are already filed from the other side (PBoC->EMU, Federal Reserve->EMU), so I did not file mirror records. The 8 October 2028 expiry is new information that the existing PBoC->EMU row does not carry, and a future round could add it in place.

checked_not_in_assignment.subject: Bank of Korea, Reserve Bank of India, Swiss National Bank, Bank of Japan / Japanese MoF
checked_not_in_assignment.text: Not separately enumerated this round, by choice. The file already holds 70 Japan records (including the bilateral swap arrangements with Indonesia, India, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand and the CMIM amendment dates), 14 Bank of Korea records and 5 Reserve Bank of India records including the SAARC framework; and all 14 CMIM participants (Brunei, Cambodia, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam) are already filed with their financial contributions and maximum arrangement amounts. The Swiss National Bank's own lines are all reciprocal halves of arrangements already filed from the other side (Fed, ECB, Bank of Canada, Bank of England, Bank of Japan, PBoC, Bank of Korea, Narodowy Bank Polski, National Bank of Belgium). Budget went to the two things that were actually missing: lapsed arrangements and the denominator.
